<em>‍</em>Selina Tewentawenron et sa sœu: ‍Selina Tewentawenron and her older sister Cecilia Etienne were kidnapped from their home by an Indian agent, an officer employed by the Government of Canada to force the assimilation of Indigenous people.
Elles ont été amenées en train au pensio: They were taken by train to Shingwauk residential school (also known as the Shingwauk Home) in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario. At the time, Selina was 6, and Cecilia was 10 or 11.
Bien qu’elle ait quitté le pensionnat il: Although she left the residential school more than seven decades ago, Selina, an Elder from Kanesatake, did not want to reveal the name of the Indian agent who kidnapped her.
« Je n’aime pas nommer le Rahetien, car: “I don’t like to name the Rahetien, because he has a family. I don’t want to upset them or hurt his family,” she says. Her daughter Brenda confirms this. “She doesn’t want to name the agent who filled out all the paperwork for her and her sister and threw them on a train at the Windsor station,” Brenda says. “If it were me, it would be a different story.”
Selina y a passé 10 ans. Elle n’est jama: Selina spent 10 years there. She never came home during that time, because her parents couldn’t pay for her ticket back. She remembers the train ride, during which, with no money and unable to speak English, she was so hungry and, of course, so frightened. It was only when she and her sister reached Blind River, Ontario, several hours from Montréal and just before the last leg of the trip, that a non-Indigenous couple who boarded the train fed them. They were left to fend for themselves, bound for an unknown destination, hearing a foreign language.
« Maman me répétait qu’à chaque fois qu’: “Mom used to tell me that every time she heard the train crossing the river – which happens often – it brought back the memory of being thrown on a train and not coming home for 10 years,” Brenda says. When she heard the news that the remains of 215 children had been found at the Kamloops residential school, Selina cried. “I felt bad and I felt pity,” she says. “A lot of thoughts came to my mind, and most of them were about me,” she says of those reflections, which she doesn’t want to share publicly.
« Quand je suis seule, ça me fait pleure: “When I’m alone, it makes me cry. Even though I think I was lucky, nothing really happened to me. Nothing worth talking about. I was too young, anyway,” Selina says. The woman, who will turn 89 in July, shares her experience alongside her daughter Brenda, who translates from Kanien’kéha into English. That part of her story is, in itself, a story of triumph.
À son arrivée à Shingwauk, Selina ne par: When she arrived at Shingwauk, Selina did not speak English. She says she got into trouble when she spoke her language, but doesn’t say more. She was immediately separated from her sister Cecilia. Some students had set up a system in which the older ones protected the younger ones, and sometimes other children too. Within four years, Selina managed to learn functional English by reading books, listening to other students and paying attention to what the clergy said. Hunger and isolation were common.
« Nous ne pouvions aller nulle part et n: “We couldn’t go anywhere and we did what we were told to do,” says the woman in her eighties. She considers herself lucky to have had other people to help her throughout her time there, including a number of students from Kanesatake. One student in particular, Morris Bonspille, arrived at Shingwauk a few weeks after she did. “He was always worried about me. He was on the boys’ side and I was on the girls’ side, but he saw me as a sister,” Selina recalls. “He was a very good friend.” Mr. Bonspille died in 2007.
Une fois qu’elle a maîtrisé l’anglais, S: Once she had mastered English, Selina stopped speaking her language. It was put on hold and became dormant. “When she came back, she couldn’t talk to anyone. She didn’t know any Kanien’kéha, she couldn’t even communicate with her mother,” her daughter says. “I couldn’t explain myself or do what I needed to do,” Selina says. She had to win the language back from the young people she started spending time with.
« Elle l’a réapprise, ce qui est une his: “She relearned it, which is an incredible story in itself,” Brenda says. Selina later became an elementary school teacher in the language she had fought so hard for. She remembers two girls in particular who ran away. She doesn’t know what became of them. “The teenagers used to go to parties,” she says. They went to the nearby Ojibway community of Garden River, known to hockey fans as the hometown of former NHL player and head coach Ted Nolan.
Ceux qui tentaient d’échapper à la monot: Those who tried to escape the monotony, confinement and abuse of the residential school by attending a gathering or running away were taking a great risk. If they were caught, they were punished. “When they ran away, the RCMP would catch them, bring them back and cut their hair as punishment. They were also beaten with a belt,” Selina says. Lily Nicholas is one of the Kanehsata’kehró:non who never came home. “She was buried there,” Selina remembers. “She died of pneumonia.” “At least, that’s what they told you,” her daughter adds. Mary Oke also died at Shingwauk residential school, though it isn’t known exactly what happened. Her body was brought back and buried in Kanesatake.
Malgré la vie difficile à Shingwauk, Sel: Despite the hardship of life at Shingwauk, Selina returned in 1991 with her daughter for a reunion. “I took my mother up there because it mattered to her. She wanted one last visit,” Brenda says. “I was so proud of my mother, of the respect she had for her fellow students. Many of them told me that Mom had helped them through their transition. She taught them how to survive in that system.”
